title: His son Abraham
hookLine: Abraham Maimonides wrote of intense inner devotion

lines: THE BOOKS, THE CRITICS, THE ROLE.
cards: The child of a well-known parent hears one question again and again: are you going to be just like your father? Maimonides had a son named Abraham.
He inherited his father's books, his father's critics, and, tradition says, his father's role leading the Jews of Egypt.
But when Abraham sat down to write his own great book, it wasn't another law code, and it wasn't another Guide. It was about the inside of a person at prayer.

teach.h: PRAYER WITHOUT INTENTION IS NOT PRAYER.
teach.b: His son Abraham. First, the father's line. In his law code, Maimonides wrote that prayer without kavanah, without intention, is not prayer.
A person should clear the mind, he says, and see themselves as standing before God. A law, stated in a sentence. Second, the son's book.

teach.h: A GUIDE FOR THE SERVANTS OF GOD.
teach.b: Abraham Maimonides wrote a large work in Judeo-Arabic, its title often given as a complete guide for the servants of God.

It turns that sentence about intention into a whole way of life: humility, generosity, patience, solitude, nights awake in prayer. He calls it a path, and the people walking it he calls hasidim, the devoted.
Third, the neighbors he noticed. Abraham lived among Muslims and saw the discipline of the Sufi mystics.
He wrote that some of their practices looked like what the ancient prophets of Israel once did, practices he felt his own people had lost.
So he urged praying with the whole body: bowing low, kneeling, standing in ordered rows, raising the hands. Some in his community pushed back, and the argument was real.
Fourth, a line from the Psalms that puts this kind of devotion in a few words: "I have set the LORD always before me." The father gave reasons for faith and a code for living it.
The son asked what it feels like from inside, when a person actually means the words. Both are Maimonides. One wrote the law of intention.
The other tried to live inside it.

how: Jewish prayer asks for kavanah, intention, and some people slow down at key lines, such as the first verse of the Shema, to say them with full attention.

games.why: he wrote a path of devotion, taking his father's law of intention in prayer and building a whole way of life around it.

practice: Take one line you already know by heart: if you pray, the Shema, a line from a psalm, or "I have set the LORD always before me"; if you don't, one true sentence of thanks.
Say it once, slowly, meaning each word as it passes, not faster and not twice. Then sit in the quiet it leaves behind.
